name: Neck training (flexion/extension)
lead: Neck training in the flexion and extension sense means exercising the neck forward and backward against resistance, often with a towel, hands, plate or machine. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a way to build a thicker, stronger neck that proponents say complements the jaw, physique and posture [8][12]. The neck's most visible muscles, the sternocleidomastoid on each side and the trapezius that shapes the slope into the shoulders, are the ones that give the neck its outline [18][21].

Proponents describe a chain: stronger, thicker neck muscles give a wider base under the jaw, a more balanced head-to-shoulder proportion and an upright head position, so the face reads as better supported [8][26]. Forum members also pair neck work with jaw and posture routines [26][12].

Published research on neck training mostly addresses chronic neck pain and injury reduction in sport, not appearance. Randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity strength and endurance training [1], a pilot trial tested a tailored six-week program in under-19 rugby players [2], and a systematic review and Delphi study addressed neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport [3]. No study found examined neck training for cosmetic purposes.

paras: The neck connects the head to the trunk through muscles attached to the skull, hyoid bone, clavicles and sternum [18]. The sternocleidomastoid runs obliquely across the side of the neck from the sternum and collarbone to the skull behind the ear; it is among the largest and most superficial neck muscles and is easy to see when the head turns [21]. Acting together, the two sternocleidomastoids flex the neck and extend the head, and acting alone one turns the head to the opposite side [21]. The trapezius bounds the back of the neck and shapes the slope from neck to shoulder [18].

Forward and backward movements load the flexors at the front, including the sternocleidomastoids and deeper muscles, and the extensors at the back [21]. An MRI study of ten adult men and ten ten-year-old boys fitted a power-law relationship between neck circumference and the cross-sectional area of six neck muscle groups, giving a way to relate the outer measurement of the neck to the muscle inside it [22]. Wikipedia attributes the larger average neck circumference of men mainly to muscle mass and body composition [18].

Forum guides describe the two core movements as a forward curl that works the front of the neck and a backward extension that works the back, often with a towel over the head for comfort [8]. People use a towel, their own hands for resistance, a weight plate, a head harness, or a neck machine, and some also include side movements [8][9]. In a reply to that guide, one member said slow, stretch-focused repetitions can work without added weight [8].

Neck work in sport is established in contact and combat sports. A randomized pilot trial in 34 male rugby players aged 16 to 18 used a tailored six-week neck conditioning program [2]. A 2021 systematic review of strength and conditioning protocols for neck strength found three studies, all in male athletes, two of which reported significant gains in isometric neck strength; the authors concluded evidence was insufficient to say that strengthening reduces impact injury risk in adult sport [15].

Members commonly discuss neck work alongside jaw and posture routines. Forum thread titles include a post arguing that neck training is needed for people who have built a wider face or sharper jawline but still have a thin neck, an advice thread on high versus low repetitions, and threads of progress photos [26][27][28]. Forward head posture, which Wikipedia describes as the head sitting forward of the shoulders with the chin jutting forward, is a recurring concern, and its suggested exercises include strengthening the deep front neck muscles and shoulder-blade retractors [19].

A randomized study of 180 women with chronic neck pain assigned participants to high-intensity strength training, local muscle endurance training or a control group, and evaluated changes in neck strength, pain and disability, with a one-year follow-up [1]. Wikipedia reports that strengthening exercises may improve function and pain in neck pain and that craniocervical flexion exercises are reported as effective for chronic neck pain without a specific cause, adding that the wording of the evidence is tentative in places [20]. Other work has explored how experimental neck pain and training affect motor cortex excitability [4][5][6].

A 2014 study measured neck strength and circumference in 6,704 US high school athletes across 51 schools and followed them for concussion; smaller neck circumference and weaker neck strength were associated with concussion, and each extra pound of neck strength was associated with 5% lower odds of concussion after adjustment [13]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies with 7,625 participants found that five studies linked greater neck strength or motor control to lower concussion incidence, but pooled effects were small and non-significant with very low certainty of evidence [14]. A prospective cohort of 136 professional rugby players found that neck strength did not predict concussion in a clinically meaningful way [16]. A 2023 analysis examined injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and soccer head and neck injuries [7], and a 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus study addressed neck training to reduce head acceleration events [3]. A pilot study evaluated a neuromuscular neck training device for multiplanar neck strength [29].

Because neck circumference is easy to measure, it has been studied as a health marker. In 1,912 Turkish adults, neck circumference averaged 36.7 cm, and each one-standard-deviation increase was associated with metabolic syndrome and with obstructive sleep apnea [24]. In 3,942 sleep clinic patients, neck-to-height ratio was the strongest predictor of apnea severity, explaining 19% of its variability [23]. These studies measure total neck size, which includes fat as well as muscle, and do not address muscle growth from training. A 2014 case report described a 37-year-old man with weightlifting-related neck muscle hypertrophy who developed head-turn-triggered near-fainting from vertebral artery occlusion; the authors discussed whether muscle bulk might affect vertebral artery flow [17].

A forum guide presents neck exercises as giving a thicker, stronger neck that goes with the physique, could improve posture and a 'high T' look [8]. Other threads ask about frequency and repetitions, whether training one side more would cause asymmetry, and why months of training showed no visible change [9][10]. A 2019 thread titled around sleep apnea indicates that members also discuss possible airway concerns [11].

Thread titles on looksmax.org also ask for 'neck training for better looks', share before-and-after neck photos and compare routines [12][26][12]. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places such practices among the milder softmaxxing and fitness end of the scene, as distinct from surgical or unconventional routes [30].
No studies found on neck flexion and extension training for cosmetic appearance. Trials exist for chronic neck pain [1] and for sport populations [2][3][7], but they do not measure looks.

lore.intro: Neck training is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, discussed as a way to improve overall look and sometimes as a complement to jaw work [8][12][26].

claims.claim: A thicker neck improves overall looks and physique
claims.believers: Guide authors say a thicker, stronger neck suits the physique and gives a high-testosterone look [8].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined neck size and perceived attractiveness in this context.

claims.believers: A forum guide says neck exercises improve posture over time [8].
claims.experts: Trials in neck pain report effects on strength, pain and disability [1]; posture-for-appearance claims have not been tested.

claims.claim: Training one side more can make the neck asymmetrical
claims.believers: A member answered a poster's question by saying that uneven training would produce asymmetry [9].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this question for cosmetic neck training.

claims.claim: Neck training can cause sleep apnea
claims.believers: A thread title raises the concern [11].
claims.experts: No studies have addressed this question.

claims.claim: Neck training widens the base of the face and frames the jaw.
claims.believers: Forum thread titles argue that neck work is the missing step for someone with a wider face and better jawline but a thin neck [26].
claims.experts: No published study has examined neck muscle size and perceived facial attractiveness. Wikipedia attributes men's larger average neck size mainly to muscle mass and body composition [18].

claims.claim: Neck training reduces concussion and injury risk.
claims.believers: Contact-sport programs and neck-training devices are built on the idea that a stronger neck helps the head resist impact [2][29].
claims.experts: A 2014 high school study found each extra pound of neck strength was associated with 5% lower odds of concussion; a 2023 meta-analysis found small, non-significant pooled effects with very low certainty, and a 2021 review found insufficient evidence in adult sport [13][14][15].

claims.claim: A thicker neck is a sign of high testosterone.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says a thicker neck gives a 'high T mogger' look [8].
claims.experts: No studies found examine neck size as a signal of testosterone in this context; Wikipedia relates neck circumference to muscle mass and body composition [18].

claims.claim: Slow, stretch-focused reps work without added weight.
claims.believers: A reply in the neck guide thread says you don't need weight if you go slowly and prioritize stretch [8].
claims.experts: No published trial compares bodyweight with loaded neck training for muscle size; trials use strength and pain outcomes [1][2].

card.summary: Forward/back neck exercises for a thicker neck; well studied for pain and sport, not for looks.
card.note: Research covers pain and sport injury, not appearance.

quick.overview:
Neck training means working the neck forward and backward against resistance. Forum users promote it for a thicker neck and better posture.
Trials exist in neck pain and sport, but none test it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Resistance exercise loads the neck flexor and extensor muscles; trials in pain and sport populations measure strength, pain and range of motion.
quick.risks: No harms are documented; forum members raise questions about soreness, asymmetry and sleep apnea without published backing.

chain: Neck flexion and extension against resistance
Neck muscles are loaded and, with time, may grow
A thicker neck, with the head carried more upright, as proponents describe it
angle.text: Forum guides present neck training as a way to get a thicker, stronger neck that goes with the physique and could improve how the head is carried [8]. Resistance trials in other populations measure strength and pain rather than looks [1][2].
